claim: Individual income tax delinquent payment penalty is 0.5% of the tax not paid by the due date for each 30 days or fraction thereof the failure continues, capped at 25% of the tax due. Penalty is based on the date LDR receives the payment.
sourceDate: 2025 Form IT-540 instructions (tax year 2025, due May 15, 2026); accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: Accrual unit (30-day period, fraction rounds up), rate and cap of the individual late-pay penalty.
uncertainty: No minimum penalty stated for individual income tax (R.S. 47:1602(C)'s $3 minimum is for registration-fee failures). Statutory basis is R.S. 47:1602(A)(3); statute text was read only through a summarizer.
designImplication: Model late-pay as ceil(daysLate/30) * 0.5% of unpaid tax, capped at 25% shared with the late-file penalty.

claim: R.S. 47:1602(A)(3) sets the individual income tax failure-to-remit penalty at one-half of one percent per 30 days (versus 5% per 30 days for other taxes under (A)(2)); (A)(4) applies 0.5% per 30 days to additional tax after notice; (A)(5) caps all at 25% of the tax in the aggregate.
establishes: Statutory basis for the reduced individual-income-tax payment penalty and the aggregate cap.
uncertainty: The page was read through a summarizer, not verbatim. Subsection lettering is as the summarizer reported it.
designImplication: Individuals pay a much gentler late-pay rate than businesses, so a simulation should key the rate on tax type.

claim: The delinquent filing penalty is 5% of the tax for each 30 days or fraction thereof, calculated from the ORIGINAL due date, up to 25%. It applies only if the return is filed after the automatic extended due date (Nov 16, 2026 for TY2025). So a return filed after the extended date gets the maximum 25%. The sum of the delinquent filing and delinquent payment penalties cannot exceed 25% of the tax due.
establishes: Late-file rate, cap, the extension cliff, and that the two penalties share one 25% cap.
uncertainty: No minimum late-file penalty published for individuals.
designImplication: Model LA late-file as a cliff: zero until the extended date passes, then 25% of tax, with late-pay filling only the remaining headroom under a shared 25% ceiling.

claim: The automatic 6-month extension does not extend time to pay. Interest runs from the original due date, and late-pay penalties apply, even when the return is filed within the extension.
establishes: Filing extension and payment due date are decoupled.
designImplication: Keep separate filedOn and paidOn clocks. The extension only moves the late-file trigger.

claim: Interest on unpaid tax for Jan 1 to Dec 31, 2026 is 10.50% per year: the judicial rate of 7.50% plus 3 points, under R.S. 47:1601(A)(2). Prior years were 11.25% in 2025 and 11.75% in 2024.
url: https://dam.ldr.la.gov/lawspolicies/RIB No. 26-001  2026 Annual Interest Rate on Unpaid Taxes Final_1.pdf
establishes: The 2026 rate, set annually, and its formula.
uncertainty: The 2027 rate is not yet published.
designImplication: LA interest is one rate per calendar year. Store a year-keyed rate table.

claim: Interest is computed as days late x daily rate x amount owed. The 2026 daily rate is 0.028767% (10.5%/365), and Form R-1111 also lists a monthly rate. The worksheet applies the rate to the tax owed, with no compounding step.
sourceDate: Form R-1111 (1/26); IT-540 instructions Interest Calculation Worksheet; accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: Daily simple-interest computation on unpaid tax.
uncertainty: Neither the statute nor the forms say outright that interest is simple. 'Simple' is inferred from the worksheet's days x daily-rate method. The R-1111 table's text layout was garbled in extraction, but the 2026 daily rate 0.028767% matches 10.5%/365.
designImplication: LA interest = principal * 0.105 * days/365, with no compounding.

claim: Whether LA charges interest on penalties: no official LDR or statutory statement found. R.S. 47:1601 (as summarized) does not address it, and the IT-540 worksheet applies interest to the tax owed.
establishes: NOT FOUND
uncertainty: An LDR FAQ page, as rendered by a summarizer, implied that interest is not computed on penalties. That is an inference, not a quote.
designImplication: Default to interest on tax only for LA, and keep this flag configurable.

claim: Interest is imposed by law and ordinarily cannot be waived. It accrues from the original due date until the liability is paid in full.
establishes: Interest is non-waivable. Penalties can be waived for reasonable cause under R.S. 47:1603.
designImplication: A penalty-abatement mechanic should never remove interest on tax.

claim: Individual installment agreement: apply through LaTAP, by email, or on Form R-19026 by mail. The non-refundable fee is $105, and there is no fee if Louisiana AGI is $25,000 or less. A 20% down payment may be required. Payments are equal monthly amounts by required automatic bank debit. Penalty, interest and collection fees keep accruing.
establishes: Fee, down payment, payment mechanics and how to apply.
uncertainty: The form gives no maximum number of months. A 2025 proposed rule would let the fee be paid in installments, but its final status was not verified.
designImplication: A plan needs a down payment of 20% of the balance and a $105 fee unless income is low, and interest keeps running on the plan balance.

claim: Under LAC 61:I.4919(D), informal installment agreements are allowed only if the amount owed is under $25,000 and the term is 36 months or less. A formal agreement, with financial disclosure, is required at $25,000 or more or for terms over 36 months.
sourceDate: Louisiana Administrative Code, May 2024 compilation (LR 47:893, July 2021; amended LR 50:1293, Sept 2024)
establishes: The streamlined-plan ceiling of under $25,000 and 36 months, with a higher-friction formal path above it.
uncertainty: No absolute maximum term is stated for formal agreements. R-19026 asks only for the 'number of months requested'.
designImplication: Use two plan tiers: auto-approve under $25k and up to 36 months, and require a financial review above that.

claim: Default: if any installment is not paid on or before its date, the whole outstanding balance becomes due immediately on notice and demand, and all collection actions resume. There is no grace or cure period. Reinstatement takes taxpayer request, secretary approval and a mandatory $60 fee. If the plan has been cancelled 90 days or longer, a new $105 fee applies instead. No fees apply if LA AGI is $25,000 or less. An NSF debit also cancels the plan and adds an NSF fee.
establishes: Missed-payment handling and reinstatement cost.
uncertainty: The NSF fee amount is not given on the form.
designImplication: One missed LA installment flips the plan to defaulted. Offer a paid reinstatement action ($60, or $105 after 90 days).

claim: The taxpayer must stay current: failing to file all required returns, or to pay all taxes that come due during the plan, is a default, so the whole balance becomes due. A new balance does not join the existing plan.
establishes: A new liability during a plan is a default trigger, not an add-on.
uncertainty: LDR could presumably set up a new or revised agreement after reinstatement, but no published procedure says so.
designImplication: When a new year's balance appears mid-plan, require full payment or default the plan.

claim: Refunds are offset during a plan. All state tax refunds are applied to the debt until it is paid in full, and federal refund offsets (less the IRS offset fee) are credited too. Offsets do not reduce or postpone any scheduled installment. An approved plan does not prevent garnishment of IRS or LDR refunds.
establishes: Offsets continue during a plan and do not count as installments.
designImplication: Apply refund offsets to the plan balance (shortening the plan) without crediting the monthly installment due.

claim: A state tax lien may be filed if the tax due is over $2,500 and/or payments run longer than 12 months. Taxpayers should keep paying monthly even before LDR approves the plan.
establishes: Thresholds at which a plan carries a lien.
uncertainty: 'May be filed' means discretionary.
designImplication: Attach a lien flag to plans over $2,500 or 12 months.

claim: Decision time for an installment request: not published. The form says only that LDR will notify the taxpayer on approval.
establishes: NOT FOUND
designImplication: Pick a modelled approval latency and label it as an assumption.

claim: For a non-filer or federal-state match case, LDR's sequence is: questionnaire; 30-day Proposed Assessment; 60-day Formal Assessment; Statement of Account (notice of seizable status); Notice of Intent to Offset and/or Suspend Licenses. If the debt is not paid within 60 days of the Notice of Intent to Offset, it is submitted to the U.S. Treasury Offset Program and may be assigned to a collection agency.

steps: Notice of Intent to Offset / Suspend Licenses (60 days)

establishes: The ordered notice ladder and the day counts between steps.
uncertainty: The presentation is from 2017. The 2026 LDR web pages name a Notice of Proposed Assessment, Notice of Assessment and Notice of Final Assessment, but give no day counts.
designImplication: Drive collections as a state machine: proposed (30d), then assessed (60d), then final/seizable, then offset notice (60d), then TOP and agency referral.

claim: Under R.S. 47:1565, the notice of assessment gives 60 calendar days to pay or appeal to the Board of Tax Appeals. With no appeal, the assessment becomes final and collectible by distraint and sale. 2026 SB 196 (enrolled) changes 60 to 90 days for notices mailed on or after Jan 1, 2028.
sourceDate: R.S. 47:1565 history through Acts 2024, No. 307; SB 196 (2026 RS) enrolled text https://www.legis.la.gov/legis/ViewDocument.aspx?d=1468441
establishes: When an assessment becomes final and enforceable.
uncertainty: SB 196 is the enrolled version. Whether the governor signed it was not verified.
designImplication: Levy and garnishment are only legal after the 60-day window (90 days from 2028).

claim: Once a debt is collectible by distraint and sale, LDR must send a notice that, if the debt is not paid within 60 days, a collection fee of up to 25% of the total liability will be charged. Where the Attorney General takes the account, the fee may not exceed 15%. The fee goes to the collection contractor. (SB 196 would make this 90 days from 2028.)
establishes: The size and trigger of the LA collection fee.
uncertainty: The actual percentage currently charged by LDR's private contractor is not published. 25% is the ceiling, not necessarily the rate. Separately, the Office of Debt Recovery charges 15% on non-tax agency debts referred on or after Jan 1, 2024 (LAC 61:III.3101), which may not apply to LDR tax debts.
designImplication: Add a one-time collection fee of up to 25% of total liability 60 days after the final-assessment collection notice. Treat the rate as a parameter.

claim: LDR collection tools include wage garnishment, bank levy, tax liens, LA and federal refund offsets, driver's and hunting/fishing license suspension, outside collection agency, and merchant-service-provider levy. A collection notice explaining the amount and options is sent before any action. Receiving a collection notice does not by itself mean immediate garnishment or levy.
establishes: The menu of enforcement tools.
uncertainty: No day counts are given for when levy or garnishment starts after the final assessment.
designImplication: Enforcement events should require a prior notice event in the log.

claim: Exact number of days from final assessment to the first bank levy or wage garnishment: not published.
establishes: NOT FOUND
designImplication: Use an assumed lag after the 'seizable' Statement of Account.

claim: If a taxpayer fails to file, the secretary determines the tax, penalty and interest by estimate or otherwise. The secretary mails a notice of that determination and states the intent to assess it after 30 calendar days from the notice date (R.S. 47:1562). LDR's federal-state match finds residents who filed federally but not with LA, sends a questionnaire, and creates a bill if there is no response.
sourceDate: R.S. 47:1562 history through Acts 2006, No. 34; 2017 LDR liaison deck
establishes: How and when a non-filer gets an estimated assessment.
uncertainty: The federal-state match details come from a 2017 presentation. No separate non-filer penalty beyond the 25% late-file maximum was found.
designImplication: A non-filing resident gets an estimated bill (tax from federal data, plus a 25% late-file penalty and interest), then follows the normal assessment ladder.

claim: General rule: installment agreement payments are 'applied to accounts, taxes, and periods as determined by the department' (LAC 61:I.4919(B)(7)). The only published fixed order (tax, then penalty, then interest, oldest period first) appears in the 2014 amnesty rule, for payments under voided amnesty installment agreements.
establishes: There is no general published allocation order. Tax-penalty-interest is the order LDR used in its amnesty rule.
uncertainty: Applying the amnesty order generally is an extrapolation.
designImplication: Default to oldest period first, then tax, penalty, interest, and flag it as an assumption.

claim: LDR applies LA income tax refunds to eligible debts under the Louisiana Tax Offset Garnishment Act. Debts include LDR tax liabilities and other agency debts (child support, overpayments, fees, fines) collected through the Office of Debt Recovery. Federal offsets are run separately by Treasury.
establishes: State refund offset to state debts.
designImplication: Net any LA refund against open LA balances before paying it out.

claim: LDR participates in the U.S. Treasury Offset Program. If full payment is not received within 60 days of the Notice of Intent to Offset, LDR submits the liability to TOP to offset federal refunds.
sourceDate: LDR Collection Division liaison presentation, 2017; corroborated by LAC 61:I.4919(C)(2) (federal refund offsets credited less IRS fee)
establishes: LA tax debts can take federal refunds after a 60-day notice.
uncertainty: A search snippet attributed to a now-404 LDR 'treasury-refund-offsets' page said the assessment must be more than 180 days and less than 10 years old. That could not be verified on an official page.
designImplication: After the 60-day offset notice, an LA debt can intercept the player's federal refund, less a TOP fee.

claim: Multistate or reciprocal state-to-state refund offset agreements for LA: none found on official LDR or legislature sources.
establishes: NOT FOUND
designImplication: Do not model LA refunds offsetting other states' debts unless a source is found.

claim: Failure to pay tax shown on a return (G.L. c. 62C, s.33(b)): 1% of the unpaid tax per month or fraction thereof, up to 25% in the aggregate. Each month it is computed on the tax shown minus amounts paid before that month began.
establishes: Late-pay rate, accrual unit, cap, and that partial payment reduces the base.
uncertainty: No minimum penalty.
designImplication: Recompute MA late-pay monthly on the remaining unpaid tax, stopping at 25% of tax shown.

claim: Failure to pay a deficiency assessment within 30 days of the Notice of Assessment (s.33(c)): 1% per month or fraction, up to 25% of the assessed tax. DOR's penalty table says this is 'combined with section 33(b)'. The penalty is waived during the first 30 days and while an abatement or appeal is pending.
sourceDate: Page updated January 28, 2025 (read via web.archive.org snapshot 2026-06-06, since mass.gov returned 403 to direct fetch); 830 CMR 62C.33.1(5)(e)
establishes: A second late-pay penalty on billed deficiencies.
uncertainty: Exactly how s.33(b) and s.33(c) combine under one 25% cap is stated only as 'combined with section 33(b) above'.
designImplication: For audit-generated bills, start the 1%/month clock 30 days after the notice.

claim: Failure to file by the due date or extended due date (s.33(a)): 1% per month or fraction thereof of the tax required to be shown (minus timely payments and credits), up to 25%. It stops accruing when the return is filed, at 25%, or when DOR assesses for the missing return. The late-file and late-pay penalties are separate, each capped at 25%, so together they can reach 50% of unpaid tax.
sourceDate: AP 612, dated 01/24/2024 (via web.archive.org snapshot 2026-01-16); G.L. c. 62C s.33(a); 830 CMR 62C.33.1(5)(c)
establishes: Late-file mechanics, and that MA stacks the penalties while LA shares one cap.
uncertainty: The 50% combined figure is derived from the separate caps, not stated as a number by DOR. DOR's FAQ says the penalties are 'each capped at 25 percent of the unpaid tax'.
designImplication: MA late-file and late-pay run in parallel, 2%/month combined, each saturating at 25%.

claim: The underpayment rate is the federal short-term rate plus 4 points, compounded daily (G.L. c. 62C s.32(a)), and is set quarterly. 2026 rates: Q1 8%, Q2 7%, Q3 8%. Q4 2026 is reported as 8% (TIR 26-5).
sourceDate: TIR 26-3 dated May 27, 2026 (via web.archive.org snapshot 2026-09-18); Q4 from TIR 26-5
establishes: Current rates and the compounding rule.
uncertainty: The Q4 2026 8% rate comes from a web-search summary of TIR 26-5. mass.gov blocked direct fetch and no archive snapshot existed, so it is unverified against the page.
designImplication: Compound MA interest daily at a quarter-keyed rate, unlike LA's simple annual rate.

claim: Interest is charged on unpaid penalties as well as unpaid tax, at the same rate, compounded daily. On the late-file penalty it runs from the due date (or extended due date) to payment. On the s.33(b)/(c) late-pay penalties it runs from 31 days after the notice of assessment. Interest cannot be waived or abated except as a result of a tax or penalty abatement.
sourceDate: 830 CMR 62C.33.1(6) (via web.archive.org 2026 snapshot); G.L. c. 62C s.32(c)
establishes: Interest compounds on penalties too.
designImplication: MA balances snowball: penalty buckets also accrue daily-compounded interest.

claim: Payment agreements: for liabilities of $10,000 or less, apply online in MassTaxConnect or by phone, for up to 36 months, minimum $25/month. For $10,001 or more, call Collections; Form M-433(I) financials may be required and the minimum is $50/month. Payments can be weekly, bi-weekly or monthly by EFT, check or money order (no card). A Notice of Assessment or Statement of Account must have been issued first, so a taxpayer at the NIA stage must wait.
establishes: Plan tiers, terms, minimums and eligibility timing.
uncertainty: An older DOR FAQ (updated April 30, 2025) says most taxpayers owing under $5,000 can apply online and that agreements generally may not exceed 36 months. The $10,000 figure is the newer one.
designImplication: Self-serve plan only after the bill is issued: 36 months maximum and $25/month minimum for balances up to $10k.

claim: Setup fee for an MA payment agreement: none stated on official DOR pages (AP 631, the payment agreement FAQ, or the collections FAQ).
establishes: NOT FOUND
uncertainty: The absence of a stated fee is not proof that there is no fee.
designImplication: Model the MA plan fee as $0 and label it as an assumption.

claim: All outstanding returns must be filed before a plan is considered. A down payment is usually required. Penalties and interest keep accruing, though AP 612.5 says the late-pay penalty may be waived once a payment agreement is entered. The plan extends the collection statute of limitations. A lien may be filed unless the repayment is accelerated (DOR describes a 12-month lien-waiver agreement, per secondary sources). The taxpayer remains subject to intercepts and offsets: refunds from earlier or later years are offset to the liability during the plan.
sourceDate: AP 631 dated 01/30/2026 (via web.archive.org snapshot 2026-06-07); 'Understanding an audit or collection activity' updated April 30, 2025
establishes: Plan conditions, and that refund offsets continue.
uncertainty: The 12-month lien-waiver figure came only from a web-search summary, not an official page read in full. The down payment amount is not specified.
designImplication: In MA, entering a plan can freeze the late-pay penalty but not interest. Offsets still sweep refunds.

claim: Default: a missed payment triggers a Notice of Intent to Cancel Payment Agreement. If the missed installment is not paid 'promptly', the plan is cancelled and the full balance is due, with levy and seizure possible. Failing to file current returns or pay current taxes during the plan also triggers the notice. The taxpayer must file and pay immediately, so a new balance must be paid in full, not added to the plan. Reinstatement can be requested by phone after a cancellation notice.
establishes: A two-step default (intent-to-cancel notice, then cancellation), unlike LA's immediate default.
uncertainty: The cure period in days is not published.
designImplication: Give MA plans a warning state between a missed payment and cancellation, and have new liabilities trigger the same warning.

claim: Decision time for a payment agreement request: not published. The FAQ only says collection activity may continue until the agreement is approved.
establishes: NOT FOUND
designImplication: Keep enforcement live during a pending plan application.

claim: Bill sequence: an optional Notice of Intent to Assess (30 days to request a pre-assessment conference, G.L. c. 62C s.26(b)); a Notice of Assessment (pay within 30 days, or apply for abatement within 60 days for a deficiency); a Statement of Account (2nd bill, a demand for payment); then a Notice of Collection or Final Notice from the Collections Bureau. Enforcement can start once a Statement of Account has been issued and 60 days have passed since the assessment. By statute, levy is allowed if the tax is unpaid 10 days after demand (s.53).
sourceDate: DOR collections process page (via web.archive.org snapshot 2026-05-15); AP 610 dated 01/27/2025; G.L. c. 62C ss.26, 53
establishes: The ordered notices and the day gates before enforcement.
uncertainty: The exact days between the Statement of Account and the Final Notice are not published.
designImplication: MA state machine: NIA (30d), then NOA (30d to pay), then SOA (10d), then enforcement eligible at 60 days after assessment.

claim: Enforcement tools: bank levy, wage levy (continuous until paid), 60-day levies on other property, liens (a Notice of Massachusetts Tax Lien, effective 10 years from assessment), state and federal refund intercepts, lottery and casino intercepts, driver's license and registration suspension (Notice of Intent to Suspend, 30 days, then RMV suspends 10 days after marking), professional license non-renewal (30 days to respond), public disclosure for debts of $25,000 or more delinquent 6 months (90 days after notice), seizure (Notice of Intent to Seize, 10 days), and outside collection agency (taxpayer notified at least 30 days before referral).
sourceDate: AP 631 dated 01/30/2026 (via web.archive.org); 'Understanding an audit or collection activity' updated April 30, 2025
establishes: Timings for each escalation tool.
designImplication: Each MA enforcement action has its own notice timer, so the game can show them escalating in parallel.

claim: MA collection costs: a $30 demand charge per demand for payment missed (G.L. c. 62C s.46 and c. 60 s.15), plus levy and seizure expenses recoverable from the taxpayer (s.53). A dishonored payment costs 2% if $1,500 or more, otherwise the lesser of $30 or the payment amount.
establishes: MA's collection fees are flat charges, not a percentage.
designImplication: Add a $30 fee each time a demand bill goes unpaid. No percentage surcharge.

claim: Percentage fee or surcharge charged to the taxpayer when an MA account is referred to an outside collection agency: not found on official sources.
establishes: NOT FOUND
uncertainty: AP 631.7 cites G.L. c. 14 s.3A authority and the notice requirement but no fee.
designImplication: Do not add an agency-referral surcharge in MA without a source.

claim: For a failure to file, DOR may assess at any time, without a Notice of Intent to Assess, using its best information and belief (s.26(d)); there is no statute of limitations. If the taxpayer was notified of the failure to file and does not file a proper return within 30 days, DOR may assess up to DOUBLE the tax determined (s.28), on top of other penalties. DOR generally requires the current year plus 6 prior years to be filed.
sourceDate: accessed 2026-10-11; also AP 612.7 and 'Understanding an audit or collection activity' (updated April 30, 2025)
establishes: The non-filer path and the double-assessment sanction.
uncertainty: 'Up to' double is discretionary.
designImplication: A non-filer who ignores the MA notice for 30 days can face 2x tax, plus 25% late-file, late-pay, and compounding interest.

claim: Without written taxpayer instructions (Form TDP-1 or a letter with the payment), DOR applies a payment first by tax type (in a published order), then by tax period in chronological order, then within a period to tax, penalties and interest in that order. DOR may adjust the order when a liability nears the collection statute of limitations. Involuntary payments (levy, distraint) cannot be directed.
establishes: The default allocation waterfall.
designImplication: Allocate MA payments oldest year first, then tax, penalty, interest. Optionally let the player direct voluntary payments.

claim: DOR applies overpayments to outstanding undisputed tax liabilities, even if the taxpayer asked for the overpayment to be credited to next year's estimated tax (AP 606.1; G.L. c. 62C s.36). A $10 fee is deducted per intercept, and up to $25 for Comptroller (other agency) intercepts. Offset priority: (i) state tax, (ii) child support, (iii) federal income tax (IRS levy), (iv) Medicaid child health costs, (v) unemployment overpayments, then other certified debts.
establishes: Self-offset, the fee, and the priority order.
designImplication: When intercepting an MA refund, deduct the $10 fee first, then apply the remainder to state tax debts before other claimants.

claim: Treasury Offset Program: the Commissioner and the State Comptroller may enter a Reciprocal Offset Agreement with Treasury. MA submits state tax liabilities to be offset against federal payments to vendors and contractors, and federal non-tax debts are offset against MA tax refunds. AP 606.7 authorizes reciprocal offset agreements with other states, a separate agreement per state, and a fee may apply. AP 631 adds that delinquent taxpayers are subject to interception of 'state and/or federal refunds'.

value.treasuryOffsetProgram: reciprocal agreement (federal vendor payments; federal refunds per AP 631)

establishes: MA participates in TOP and is authorized to enter multistate offset agreements.
uncertainty: Which states, if any, MA actually has reciprocal offset agreements with: NOT FOUND. Whether MA tax debts are offset against federal income tax refunds specifically (versus vendor payments) is stated only generally in AP 631.
designImplication: Treat a cross-state refund offset as possible in MA but unconfirmed for any specific partner state.

claim: Failure to pay tax when due (without intent to evade): one-time penalty of 5% of the tax, for taxes assessed on or after 2023-01-01. Not monthly, no cap beyond the flat 5%.
establishes: G.S. 105-236(a)(4), version effective until July 1, 2027; confirmed by NCDOR Penalties and Fees Overview
uncertainty: Low. Statute text read directly.
designImplication: Model NC late payment as a single flat 5% charge at the due date, not a growing meter.

claim: From July 1, 2027 the failure-to-pay penalty becomes 2% per month or fraction of a month, capped at 10% in aggregate.
establishes: Scheduled change in G.S. 105-236(a)(4) (future version) and NCDOR overview
uncertainty: Low on text; whether it applies by assessment date or tax period is not stated on the page.
designImplication: A simulation spanning 2027 can switch NC late payment from flat to monthly accrual by date, a built-in rule-change event.

claim: No minimum dollar amount for the failure-to-pay penalty appears in G.S. 105-236(a)(4).
establishes: Absence of a minimum in the current statute text
uncertainty: Medium: absence read from a fetched summary of the section.
designImplication: No floor needed for NC penalties; small debts get small penalties.

claim: Failure to file by due date (with extension): 5% of the tax for the first month or less, plus 5% for each additional month or fraction, not exceeding 25% in aggregate.
uncertainty: Low.
designImplication: Late filing grows 5%/month to 25% after five months: a clear incentive to file even when unable to pay.

claim: Late-filing and late-payment penalties both apply (stack) when a return is filed late with tax due; there is no offset of one against the other.
establishes: NCDOR overview states both penalties can apply to the same month and are assessed together
uncertainty: Medium: the 30% combined maximum is my arithmetic (25% + 5%), not a published figure.
designImplication: NC penalties add; max penalty exposure on unfiled-and-unpaid tax is 30% under current law.

claim: Interest rate on assessments and refunds is 7% per year for both halves of 2026 (Jan-Jun and Jul-Dec); it was 7% throughout 2025 and 8% in 2024.
establishes: NCDOR interest rate table under G.S. 105-241.21
uncertainty: Low.
designImplication: Use 7%/yr for NC 2026; rates move in six-month steps.

claim: Secretary sets the rate by June 1 and December 1 for six-month periods starting July 1 and January 1; floor 5%, ceiling 16% per year. Interest accrues from the statutory payment date until paid, only on principal tax, never on penalty.
establishes: G.S. 105-241.21: 'Interest accrues only on the principal of the tax and does not accrue on any penalty.'
uncertainty: Low.
designImplication: Interest base is tax principal only; penalties are a static add-on.

claim: Whether NC interest is simple or compound, and whether computed daily or monthly, is not stated in G.S. 105-241.21 or the NCDOR interest pages.
establishes: NOT FOUND
uncertainty: High. Statute says interest accrues on principal and not on penalty, which implies no compounding on interest, but not stated.
designImplication: Model as simple interest on principal (safest reading), flag as assumption.

claim: Installment Payment Agreement available after receiving a Notice of Collection, final bill or final determination; maximum 18 monthly installments under the standard criteria; no stated maximum balance. Exceptions requested via Form RO-1062 with 3 months of bank statements.
establishes: NCDOR Installment Payment Agreements page
uncertainty: Low on 18 months; longer terms possible by exception with no stated limit.
designImplication: Cap standard NC plans at 18 months; longer plans need an exception path with financial disclosure.

claim: Eligibility: all required returns filed (or assessed), no prior default on same periods, no active collection warrant or bank garnishment, not under criminal investigation, bank draft required, term within statute of limitations. Apply online with Form RO-1033. Review time not guaranteed.
establishes: NCDOR eligibility list
uncertainty: Decision time NOT FOUND (Department says it cannot guarantee review length).
designImplication: Plan eligibility should check filing compliance and absence of active garnishment.

claim: Setup fee for an NC installment agreement: none stated on the official page.
establishes: NOT FOUND (no fee published)
uncertainty: Absence of a fee is not stated explicitly.
designImplication: Treat NC plan setup as free unless a source shows otherwise.

claim: During the plan, interest continues to accrue, the Department offsets any state or federal tax refunds and NC Education Lottery winnings, and the 20% collection assistance fee is waived while the agreement is current (if not already assessed).

Notice of Collection - Amount Shown Due But Not Paid In Full (N0002401/N0002402)

claim: Order in which a partial income tax payment is applied (tax vs penalty vs interest) is not published for individual income tax. G.S. 105-358(b) (penalties, interest, costs first, then principal) is in the Machinery Act and governs property tax, not income tax.
establishes: NOT FOUND for income tax

claim: Penalty for failure to pay (negligence, no intent to evade): 2% per month or any fraction of a month from the due date on tax due but not paid, not to exceed 20%.

claim: Interest equals the IRC section 6621 underpayment rate for individuals, set quarterly, accrued daily from the day after the due date until paid. 2026: Jan 1-Mar 31 7% (0.019178082%/day); Apr 1-Jun 30 6% (0.016438356%/day); Jul 1-Dec 31 7% (0.019178082%/day). uncertainty: Low.

sourceDate: statute current as of 2024-01-01 per FindLaw; accessed 2026-10-11

claim: Two tiers: short-term payment plans of 12 or fewer installments, no lien; installment agreements of 13 to 72 months that require a lien or acceptable security. Self-service setup on Taxpayer Access Point (TAP), choosing down payment and duration up to 72 months.

claim: Default triggers: missed minimum payment, late payment, establishing new debt, or not timely filing returns. Short-term plan: a missed payment terminates the agreement and collection proceeds. claim: Notices: Notice of Assessment or Statement of Account; taxpayer becomes delinquent if the assessment is not paid, protested or secured within 90 days of assessment or demand; then Notice of Intent to Lien or Final Notice Before Seizure; Notice of Claim of Tax Lien (Section 7-1-37); Notice of Intent to Outsource before referral to a collection agency.

claim: Levy by warrant of levy (Section 7-1-31) on delinquent taxpayers: financial institutions must immediately surrender property; employers surrender wages above the amount exempt under Section 7-1-36. Exact wage exemption amount or percent not retrieved.

establishes: NOT FOUND

claim: TRD mails notices to non-filers; on IRS information it estimates personal income tax from federal AGI (or 1099 data) and issues a Notice of Assessment for tax, the 7-1-69 penalty and interest. claim: TRD intercepts PIT refunds to pay outstanding state tax liabilities, and under the Tax Refund Intercept Program Act transfers refunds to agencies for child support, student loans, unemployment overpayments, court debts and workers' compensation. claim: A one-time delinquency penalty of 5% of unpaid tax applies when tax is not paid (or a return not filed) by the due date; it applies even if an extension to file was obtained.

uncertainty: Low. DOR page https://www.oregon.gov/dor/programs/individuals/pages/penalties.aspx (accessed 2026-10-11, undated) confirms 5% even with extension.

claim: No minimum dollar amount for the 5% penalty was found. Payment is not required if the balance due on the return is under $1.

uncertainty: Minimum penalty NOT FOUND in ORS 314.400 or on the DOR penalties page.

claim: The 5% penalty is not imposed if, after an amended return with short payment or a deficiency notice, the taxpayer pays full tax plus accrued interest within 30 days of the date on DOR's notice.

uncertainty: Low.

claim: If an annual return is filed more than 3 months after the due date (including extensions), a 20% failure-to-file penalty is added on top of the 5% penalty, for a combined 25% of unpaid tax.

uncertainty: Low. DOR penalties page (accessed 2026-10-11) states the combined total is 25 percent.

claim: If returns are not filed for 3 consecutive years by the due date (incl. extensions) of the third year's return, a penalty of 100% of the tax liability (after credits and prepayments) is imposed for each such year, in addition to other penalties.
sourceDate: ORS 2025 edition, ORS 305.992 (amended 2025 c.371 s.7); accessed 2026-10-11

uncertainty: Low. Confirmed on DOR penalties page (accessed 2026-10-11).

claim: Total penalties under ORS 305.992, 305.265(13) and 314.400 for any tax year may not exceed 100% of the tax liability/deficiency.

uncertainty: Low.

claim: A 100% penalty on any deficiency applies for failure to file, or false filing, with intent to evade tax (fraud).

uncertainty: Low.

claim: Interest on deficiencies and delinquencies for interest periods beginning on or after 2026-01-01 is 8% per year (Tier One); daily rate = annual/365 without rounding (about 0.0219% per day). The same rate applies to refunds. The rate is based on the IRS third-quarter underpayment rate.
establishes: 2026 rate and daily computation basis.
uncertainty: Low. ORBs are non-binding information; the binding rate table is OAR 150-305-0140 (not fetched).

claim: Interest is simple interest computed on a daily basis (statutory default); the director may adjust the rate by rule at most once a calendar year, taking into account the IRS underpayment rate plus 1 percentage point.

uncertainty: Low.

claim: Interest is charged on tax only; no interest is charged on penalties.
establishes: Penalties do not bear interest.

claim: Tier Two: if a deficiency is not paid within 60 days after the notice of assessment (or a short-paid return's delinquency within 60 days of assessment), the rate rises by 4 points (12% for 2026) for interest periods beginning 61 days after the notice.

designImplication: Step interest from 8% to 12% once an assessed balance is 60+ days unpaid.

claim: DOR offers payment plans up to 36 months, set up on Revenue Online or by phone (503-945-8200 for individuals). Longer terms require a Statement of Financial Condition with documentation submitted through Revenue Online. Automatic ACH payments can be linked to the plan.

uncertainty: Low for term; other plan parameters not published.

claim: Missed/default handling: DOR states it will take collection action (e.g. garnishment) if you don't make the payments you agreed to. A dishonored-payment penalty of the greater of $25 or 3x the dishonored amount (max $500) applies to 2+ dishonored payments within 2 years. The statutory notice and demand must tell the taxpayer that a warrant may be issued even if they are compliant with an installment agreement. Whether a new balance joins or defaults the plan: NOT FOUND.

uncertainty: Exact default grace period and new-balance treatment NOT FOUND.

claim: Refunds are captured and applied to debt even with a department-approved payment plan (stated for Other Agency Account debt). claim: DOR's correspondence sequence: Notice of Assessment -> Notice and Demand for Payment (second request for full payment) -> Distraint Warrant -> State Tax Lien (warrant recorded with county clerk) -> Notice of Intent to Offset Federal Income Tax Refund (certified mail) -> Notice of Intent to Offset Federal Payments -> periodic Statement of Account.

Notice of Intent to Offset Federal Payments to an Oregon Debt

claim: Written notice and demand for payment must be mailed at least 30 days before a warrant is issued; if tax is not paid within 30 days after the notice and demand, DOR may issue a warrant including penalties, interest and any collection charge. The warrant may be recorded in a county lien record, after which DOR can direct the sheriff to levy and sell property; until satisfied it has the effect of a judgment. DOR takes no action against property before a warrant (except jeopardy).

claim: Collection actions include refund offsets, wage/bank/contract-payment garnishment (Social Security and disability protected), seizure and sale of property (not primary residence), real-property tax liens, UCC liens, professional license suspension, cash-register seizure, and public listing on the Delinquent Taxpayers List for debts over $50,000.

uncertainty: Low.

claim: DOR-originated delinquent accounts must be offered to a private collection firm (PCF) no later than one year from the most recent payment (statute); DOR's OAA page says other-agency debt is assigned after six months with no payment. establishes: A PCF stage exists with a percentage fee.

claim: When a return is not filed, DOR determines the tax on best information and belief, assesses tax plus penalty and interest, and gives written notice of the failure to file and of the determination and assessment. If a return is filed before the notice of determination and assessment is issued, only the 20% failure-to-file penalty is added.

claim: All payments received are credited first to penalty, then to accrued interest, then to tax due.

claim: DOR automatically offsets the taxpayer's own state refund or overpayment against an owed balance once a balance is owed and the first bill has been sent; a Notice of Refund Offset letter is sent. claim: Hardship options: Suspended Collections status (household income under 200% of the federal poverty level, under $5,000 assets excluding home and one vehicle, non-garnishable income) stops collection actions but interest continues and refunds are offset; temporary uncollectible status; settlement offers require a 5% nonrefundable good-faith payment.

claim: A taxpayer cannot be charged both the 10% late-payment penalty (12-735(a)) and the 10%-or-$50 non-filer penalty (12-735(b)) for the same tax period. The commissioner may waive penalties for reasonable cause (12-735(c), subject to 12-3a).

claim: DRS sends a "Failure to File Notice" when its records show a filing requirement and no CT return. uncertainty: The page still names the Financial Management Service (FMS), which is now the Bureau of the Fiscal Service.
designImplication: A CT tax debt can intercept the player's federal refund 60 days after notice, with no CT fee.

claim: DRS says it receives information from other state agencies (in-state and out-of-state) and from the federal government (IRS) about outstanding liabilities, and "the law requires us to send your refund or overpayment to that agency". It notifies the taxpayer in writing.
establishes: CT state refunds can go to other states and to the IRS, which implies SITLP or reciprocal participation.
uncertainty: DRS does not name the IRS program (SITLP) or the out-of-state partners.
designImplication: A CT refund can flow out to the IRS or to another state, not only to CT creditors.

claim: CGS 12-35f authorizes reciprocal refund offsets with any "claimant state" (another state or DC) that extends like comity. Only finally due, legally enforceable taxes qualify. The taxpayer gets notice and 30 days to protest. On a protest, DRS impounds the refund and the claimant state has 45 days to recertify, or the amount is paid to the taxpayer.
establishes: The legal basis and due process for CT's side of interstate refund offsets.
uncertainty: The statute does not name partner states.
designImplication: Interstate offset: a 30-day protest window, and only final, non-appealable debts qualify.

claim: A list of the states CT has 12-35f reciprocal offset agreements with, published by CT DRS.
establishes: NOT FOUND
uncertainty: No CT DRS page listing partners was found. Counterparty official sources (the CA FTB MOP partnership page and the NY DTF refund-offsets page) each list Connecticut as a partner, so CA and NY are confirmed indirectly.
designImplication: Treat CT's partners as at least CA and NY, from the counterparties' pages.

claim: Tax Law 681(a): if a taxpayer fails to file a required return, the department may estimate NY taxable income and tax "from any information in its possession" and mail a notice of deficiency.
establishes: Statutory basis for estimated non-filer assessments.
uncertainty: Retrieved through a summarizing fetch tool (the direct download was blocked); the quoted sentence is reported by that tool.
designImplication: A NY non-filer is estimated from information returns such as W-2 and 1099 data.

claim: The first contact is the reminder letter Form AU-222 ("no record of a NYS return"). If the return is not received within 30 days of the letter, or another agreed date, the department "will determine the taxes you owe and send you a bill". A Statement of Proposed Audit Change may follow even when the taxpayer responded but the return had not arrived.

value.nextStep: Statement of Proposed Audit Change / bill

establishes: The NY non-filer letter sequence and its 30-day window.
uncertainty: How long after the due date AU-222 letters go out: NOT FOUND.
designImplication: NY pipeline: AU-222 reminder, then 30 days, then SoPAC estimate, then Notice of Deficiency.

claim: If the taxpayer still disagrees after a Statement of Proposed Audit Changes, the department issues a Notice of Determination or Notice of Deficiency. An appeal to BCMS or the Division of Tax Appeals is "generally" due within 90 days of the notice.
establishes: The appeal window after a formal notice.
uncertainty: The publication says "generally" and to refer to the notice for the applicable limit.
designImplication: After the formal notice, a 90-day appeal window, after which the assessment is fixed.

claim: Tax Law 689(b): the petition is due within 90 days of the mailing of the notice of deficiency, or 150 days if the notice is addressed to a person outside the United States.
establishes: Statutory petition window.
uncertainty: Retrieved through a summarizing fetch tool.
designImplication: Use 90 days, or 150 for a taxpayer abroad.

claim: Late-filing penalty: 5% of the tax due per month or part of a month, up to 25%. If the return is more than 60 days late, the minimum is the lesser of $100 or the total amount due on the return. The late-payment penalty is 0.5% per month, up to 25%.
establishes: The NY failure-to-file and failure-to-pay penalty schedule (Tax Law 685(a)).
uncertainty: The page does not say how 685(a)(1) and (a)(2) offset each other in months when both apply. The federal-style reduction is not confirmed here.
designImplication: NY late-file penalty = min(25%, 5% x months) with a floor of min($100, tax) after 60 days.

claim: Tax Law 685(a)(3): failure to pay tax not shown on a return within 21 calendar days of notice and demand (10 business days if $100,000 or more) adds 0.5% per month, up to 25%.
establishes: The penalty once an assessed amount is billed.
uncertainty: Retrieved through a summarizing fetch tool.
designImplication: After the bill, a 21-day grace period, then 0.5% per month.

claim: The three-year audit statute of limitations does not apply to any period for which the taxpayer failed to file a return.
establishes: Non-filers have no limitations period.
uncertainty: none
designImplication: In NY, as in CT, a non-filed year never closes.

claim: The Statewide Offset Program (SWOP): NY tax refunds may be offset for debts owed to NY state agencies, including CUNY, SUNY, the Department of Health, the Department of Labor, Higher Education, the MTA and OTDA. NY refunds are also applied to NY tax debts. Notice is Form DTF-160. A nonobligated spouse has 10 days from the DTF-160 to file IT-280 if it was not filed with the return.
establishes: NY offsets its own refunds to its own tax debts and to other state agencies' debts.
uncertainty: The agency list is "not limited to".
designImplication: A NY refund nets against NY tax debt and then other agency debts.

claim: The Federal Refund Offset Program (FROP), the TOP joint program, works both ways. The IRS may send a federal refund to NY for NY personal income tax debt, and NY may send a NY refund to the IRS for a federal tax debt. The notice is DTF-450 with 60 days to resolve or dispute. Any federal refund excess over the NY debt is returned within 60 days. Offset processing fees are deducted.
establishes: NY participates in TOP and sends its refunds to the IRS (functionally SITLP).
uncertainty: The page does not name "SITLP", and the fee amount is not stated (NOT FOUND).
designImplication: Two-way federal/NY interception; offsets carry a fee.

claim: Multistate Refund Offset Program (MOP): NY has reciprocal refund offset agreements with California, Connecticut, Delaware, Maryland and New Jersey. The notice is DTF-450 with 60 days before referral.
establishes: NY's interstate offset partners.
uncertainty: NY Publication 131 was not checked for a different list.
designImplication: An NY debtor's refunds from CA, CT, DE, MD and NJ can be pulled into NY.

claim: Other NY offsets: the Reciprocal Offset Program (ROP) with U.S. Treasury offsets federal non-tax payments for NY personal income or business tax debt (DTF-452, 60 days). The State Contract Offset Program offsets NY vendor and contract payments (DTF-650.1, 30 days). NY also offsets lottery winnings (LWOP), unclaimed funds (UCF) and SLA refunds.
establishes: NY participates in the federal State Reciprocal Program (non-tax federal payments) and several in-state payment offsets.
uncertainty: Fiscal Service does not publish a per-state SRP list. NY's ROP matches the description of SRP.
designImplication: Debt collection can reach federal vendor payments, lottery wins and unclaimed property.

claim: Request for Tax Return (FTB 4600) and Demand for Tax Return (FTB 4601): each gives 30 days from the notice date to file or reply. A Request for Information (PIT 4044) also gives 30 days if the taxpayer claims no requirement without substantiation. If there is no response to the Demand, "we'll estimate your income and issue a Notice of Proposed Assessment", including tax, a demand penalty, a delinquent filing penalty and a cost recovery fee.
establishes: The CA non-filer notice ladder and what the estimated NPA contains.
uncertainty: The time between the due date and the first 4600: NOT FOUND.
designImplication: CA ladder: 4600 (30 days), then 4601 (30 days), then an estimated NPA with stacked penalties and a fee.

claim: A Notice of Proposed Assessment may be protested within 60 days, by the "protest by" date. It becomes a bill if no action is taken. Paying in full within 15 days of the notice date stops interest.
establishes: The NPA protest window.
uncertainty: none
designImplication: A CA NPA has 60 days to contest before it becomes a final bill.

claim: Delinquent filing penalty (R&TC 19131): 5% of the tax due per month or part of a month from the original due date, up to 25%. For individuals with a balance of $540 or less, the penalty is the lesser of $135 or 100% of the amount due.
establishes: The CA failure-to-file penalty schedule.
uncertainty: The $135/$540 figures are indexed and may change by year. The statute text on leginfo.legislature.ca.gov could not be retrieved (bot-blocked), so the FTB summary is used.
designImplication: CA late-file penalty = min(25%, 5% x months), with an indexed small-balance minimum.

claim: Demand penalty (R&TC 19133): 25% of the total tax amount due, regardless of timely payments or credits, if a return is not filed by the date on the Demand for Tax Return. FTB 1140 states it is "in addition to the 25 percent late filing penalty imposed pursuant to R&TC Section 19131".
sourceDate: FTB penalties page last updated 06/17/2026; FTB 1140 revised 12/2017
establishes: A CA non-filer who ignores a demand can face up to 50% in penalties (25% + 25%).
uncertainty: Statute text not retrieved directly (leginfo was blocked). FTB 1140 is an older (12/2017) revision.
designImplication: CA is the harshest of the three: ignoring the demand doubles the penalty ceiling, and it applies even when a refund is due.

claim: Filing enforcement cost recovery fee (R&TC 19254) for failing to file in response to a legal demand: $143 for individuals and all other businesses, $122 for corporations and LLCs treated as corporations. "Fees varies year to year."
establishes: The current flat fee added to a non-filer assessment.
uncertainty: Indexed annually. This value is current as of the page date.
designImplication: Add a flat $143 enforcement fee to a CA non-filer assessment.

claim: Interagency Intercept Collections (IIC): FTB intercepts CA personal income tax refunds, lottery winnings and unclaimed property for debts owed to CA cities, schools, counties and state agencies (fines, parking citations, tolls, fees, tuition). The minimum debt is $10. Distribution follows the GC 12419.3 priority: child and family support first, then spousal support, the Restitution Fund, then EDD benefit overpayments, and so on. Taxpayers are also told unpaid CA tax may be satisfied by "interception of funds due to you from the federal government, other states, or other California state agencies".
sourceDate: IIC page last updated 09/24/2025; FTB 2645 (2026 guide) accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: CA refunds are intercepted for state and local agency debts, with a statutory priority order.
uncertainty: The application of a CA refund to the taxpayer's own FTB balance is stated only generally (FTB 1140). The specific statute was not retrieved.
designImplication: Model intercepts as a priority queue: support, then restitution, then EDD, then other agencies.

claim: FTB participates in TOP to offset federal tax refunds and federal payments for CA income tax debt. It sends an Intent to Offset Federal Payments (FTB 1102) with 60 days to pay or dispute. FTB charges a federal treasury offset fee of $23.64 (GC 16583.1) and may add a collection cost recovery fee.
sourceDate: TOP page last updated 09/24/2025; penalties page 06/17/2026
establishes: A CA tax debt reaches the federal refund, and FTB charges a fee for it (CT does not).
uncertainty: none
designImplication: The CA federal offset charges a $23.64 fee per offset; CT's is free.

claim: IIC Participation Guide (FTB 2645) cites Government Code 926.8 as authorizing the IRS to intercept funds, meaning CA refunds can go to the IRS for federal tax debt (the SITLP side).
establishes: California provides the reverse flow, from state refunds to federal debt.
uncertainty: Inferred from one citation line. FTB does not describe a SITLP program page, and an IRS list of SITLP states was NOT FOUND (the IRS levy page https://www.irs.gov/businesses/small-businesses-self-employed/federal-and-state-levy-programs lists none).
designImplication: CA refunds can be levied for federal tax debt as well.

claim: Multistate Offset Program (MOP): reciprocal agreements under the Delinquent Taxpayer Accountability Act (R&TC 19291, 19377.5, GC 12419.13) with the New York State Department of Taxation and Finance, the Connecticut Department of Revenue Services and the New Jersey Department of Treasury. The notice is FTB 4940 PC with 30 days to pay before FTB asks the partner state for the refund. Partner states charge no fees, and offsets continue during a payment plan.
establishes: CA's interstate partners. NY and CT are partners of each other and of CA, a triangle that both counterparties confirm.
uncertainty: NY lists CA as a partner, and CA lists NY. FTB lists three partners while NY lists five (CA, CT, DE, MD, NJ), because partner sets are bilateral.
designImplication: CT, NY and CA form a fully reciprocal triangle: a debt in any one can take the refund from either of the others.

claim: Federal context (applies to all three states): TOP's State Income Tax Program lets state revenue departments refer delinquent state income tax debt for offset of federal tax refunds, with $720.9M collected in FY2024. The State Reciprocal Program offsets non-tax federal payments for states with an agreement, and those states in turn offset their payments for federal debts ($76.2M in FY2024). The IRS separately runs SITLP, levying state refunds for states that participate.
sourceDate: Fiscal Service page Last Updated: January 16, 2025; IRS page accessed 2026-10-11
establishes: The federal program structure that CT, NY and CA plug into.
uncertainty: Neither Fiscal Service nor IRS publishes which states are in SRP or SITLP. A per-state list was NOT FOUND (a secondary search snippet citing "12 states in SRP" in FY2023 was not verified).
designImplication: Federal refund offset is near-universal for state tax debt; reciprocal non-tax offsets are rarer.
